title: Fed Minutes Signal Another Rate Hike Likely Before Year-End Despite Trump Pressure
excerpt: Minutes from the September 15-16 meeting show most officials saw another increase as likely by year-end, after lifting the benchmark rate to 3.75%-4.00% despite President Trump's calls for cuts.
body:
• Minutes from the Federal Reserve's September 15-16 meeting say most officials judged another rate increase would likely be appropriate by year-end.
  • The September decision lifted the benchmark rate by a quarter point to 3.75%-4.00%, about 3.9%, the first increase in more than three years.
  • Markets put about a 70% probability on a hike by year-end, with a hold expected on October 28-29 and December seen as the more likely move.
  • For borrowers, mortgage rates are already above 7% at a three-year high, so a December hike would keep home-loan and other borrowing costs elevated into 2027.

Most Federal Reserve officials expect another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year, according to minutes of the central bank's September 15-16 meeting released on October 7. The record shows policymakers agreed inflation remained elevated and had made little progress toward the Fed's 2% target in recent months, even after they raised rates at that meeting.

The September increase, approved unanimously, lifted the target range for the federal funds rate by a quarter point to 3.75%-4.00%. It was the first increase in more than three years and it came despite repeated calls from President Donald Trump for the Fed to cut rates instead. Trump criticised the rate-setting committee after the decision while still expressing support for Chair Kevin Warsh, whom he appointed earlier this year.

What the minutes show

The minutes, summarised by Realtor.com, state that most participants assessed another increase in the target range would likely be appropriate by year-end. Several officials viewed the current rate as too low to restrain the economy, or as only mildly restrictive, according to the Associated Press account of the minutes. Many officials also said financial conditions, including rising stock prices, appeared supportive of growth, a sign that tighter policy might be needed to cool demand.

Warsh made the inflation case plainly after the September meeting, saying inflation is too high and has been for too long. By the Fed's preferred measure, prices rose 3.4% in August from a year earlier, while core prices, excluding food and energy, rose 3%. On a monthly basis, overall prices rose 0.3% and core prices rose 0.2%. Officials cited higher oil and gas prices, the lingering effects of tariffs, and sharp price increases for semiconductors, computer equipment and electrical components linked to data-centre construction. Excluding some of those pressures, many officials still placed underlying inflation between 2.5% and 3%.

Why borrowing costs are already rising

Longer-term rates have climbed for reasons that go beyond the Fed's own move, including rising government debt, heavy borrowing by technology firms to finance data centres, and higher energy prices. Mortgage rates, which track the yield on the 10-year Treasury rather than the Fed's rate directly, reached 7.28% last week, a three-year high, according to Freddie Mac data cited by Realtor.com. The 10-year yield also touched its highest level in 24 years on the morning the minutes were released, before a Treasury auction steadied the market.

That distinction matters for households. A further quarter-point hike in December would not by itself set a mortgage rate, but it would reinforce the conditions keeping long-term yields high: persistent inflation, large federal borrowing and investor expectations that policy will stay tight for longer.

What happens next

Investors expect the Fed to hold steady at its October 28-29 meeting and to consider a hike in December, according to futures pricing cited by the AP and CME FedWatch data cited by Realtor.com, which put the probability of a hike by year-end at about 70%. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said last week that policymakers would need to reach their own judgement and that it may take more time, signalling no rush to move in October, which falls a week before the midterm elections.

For anyone planning a home purchase, refinance or large loan, the practical dates are October 28-29 for the next decision and the December meeting for the move markets currently expect. Until inflation moves clearly toward 2%, the minutes indicate borrowers should plan for rates to stay above recent norms rather than for a quick return to cuts.
